questions.q: R(id, v) = (1,a), (2,b), (2,c) and S(id, w) = (2,x), (2,y), (3,z). How many rows does R INNER JOIN S ON R.id = S.id return?
questions.exp: Only id = 2 matches: 2 rows in R times 2 rows in S = 4.

questions.q: The data dictionary (system catalog) of a DBMS stores
options: metadata, i.e. data about the data such as table, column and constraint definitions
questions.exp: The catalog holds metadata: schema definitions, constraints, indexes and authorizations.

questions.q: Strict two-phase locking guarantees that every schedule produced is
options: only view serializable but never conflict serializable
questions.exp: 2PL ensures conflict serializability; strict 2PL, holding exclusive locks until commit, additionally avoids cascading rollbacks. It does not prevent deadlock.

questions.q: An alternate key is
options: a foreign key that is also unique
a key that is allowed to be NULL
a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key
a key stored in a second table
questions.exp: Candidate keys not selected as the primary key are called alternate keys.

questions.q: In 2PC, every participant has voted YES and is waiting when the coordinator crashes before sending its decision. What is the position of the participants?
options: They commit automatically after a timeout because all of them voted YES
They stay blocked in the ready (uncertain) state, holding their locks, until the coordinator recovers
They abort automatically after a timeout because the coordinator failed
They elect a new coordinator, which always commits the transaction
questions.exp: A participant that has voted YES cannot decide unilaterally: the global decision may have been either commit or abort. This is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol (3PC tries to remove the blocking).

questions.q: Account A = 100. T1 reads A, T2 reads A, T1 writes A = A + 50, then T2 writes A = A + 50 (using its own earlier read). The final value of A is 150, though two additions should give 200. This anomaly is called
questions.exp: T2's write overwrites T1's update because both used the stale value 100; this is the lost update problem.

questions.q: R(P, Q, R, S) has FDs PQ → R, R → S, S → P. The candidate keys are PQ, RQ and SQ. The highest normal form of R is
questions.exp: Every attribute P, R, S is prime (part of some key), so all FDs satisfy the 3NF condition. R → S and S → P have non-superkey determinants, so BCNF fails.

questions.q: Schedule S: r1(A) w1(A) r2(A) w2(A) r1(B) w1(B). Which is correct?
options: It is conflict serializable and equivalent to the serial order T1 then T2
It is conflict serializable and equivalent to the serial order T2 then T1
It is serializable only if T2 commits first
questions.exp: The only conflicts are on A, where T1's operations precede T2's, giving the single edge T1 → T2. No cycle, so serial order T1, T2.

questions.q: Which SQL command removes all rows of a table quickly while keeping its structure for future use?
questions.exp: TRUNCATE TABLE deletes all rows and keeps the table definition; DROP TABLE removes the table itself.

questions.q: Which relational algebra operation is naturally used to answer 'find students who have enrolled in ALL courses offered by the department'?
questions.exp: Division (R ÷ S) returns values of one attribute that are associated with every tuple of S, matching 'for all' queries.

questions.q: R has 6 tuples, S has 4 tuples and R and S are union-compatible with 2 tuples in common. How many tuples does R ∪ S have?
The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee at most two of which three properties?
questions.exp: CAP: Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance; during a network partition, a system must choose between C and A.

questions.q: In log-based recovery, the main purpose of a checkpoint is to
options: reduce the amount of the log that must be scanned and processed during recovery
questions.exp: A checkpoint records a consistent state, so recovery need only examine log records after the last checkpoint (plus active transactions).

questions.q: A schedule is recoverable if
options: a transaction that reads data written by another transaction commits only after that other transaction commits
every transaction commits immediately after it starts
no two transactions access the same item
questions.exp: Recoverability requires that if Tj reads from Ti then Ti commits before Tj, so a commit never depends on an uncommitted write.

questions.q: Acc(id, bal) = (1,100), (2,200), (3,300). After UPDATE Acc SET bal = bal * 2 WHERE bal > 150; what does SELECT SUM(bal) FROM Acc return?
questions.exp: Rows 2 and 3 are doubled to 400 and 600; row 1 stays 100. Sum = 100 + 400 + 600 = 1100.

questions.q: Which DBMS component is chiefly responsible for ensuring the Isolation property of transactions?
questions.exp: Concurrency control (locking, timestamps) isolates concurrently running transactions; the recovery manager handles atomicity and durability.

questions.q: Employee(eid, name, did) has a foreign key did referencing Dept(did). An attempt to insert an employee whose did does not exist in Dept will be
options: accepted and the Dept table updated automatically
accepted with did set to NULL silently
accepted only for the first such row
rejected because it violates referential integrity
questions.exp: A non-NULL foreign key value must match an existing parent key; otherwise the DBMS rejects the insert.

questions.q: R(A, B) has 4 tuples. S(B, C) has 5 tuples with B as its primary key, and B in R is a foreign key referencing S. How many tuples does the natural join R ⋈ S contain?
questions.exp: Each R tuple matches exactly one S tuple (B is unique in S and every R.B exists in S), so the join has 4 tuples.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has the FD C → B and its only candidate key is AC. Which decomposition into BCNF is correct?
questions.exp: C → B violates BCNF (C is not a superkey). Splitting into (C, B) and (A, C) is lossless since C is a key of (C, B), and (A, C) is in BCNF.

questions.q: A relation has 4 attributes and its only candidate key is a single attribute A. How many superkeys does it have?
questions.exp: Every superkey must contain A; the other 3 attributes can be included or excluded freely, giving 2³ = 8.

questions.q: Which language is used to define the structure (schema) of a database, such as creating and altering tables?
questions.exp: Data Definition Language (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines schema; DML manipulates data.

questions.q: In an ER diagram, 'Age' computed from 'Date_of_birth' is an example of a
questions.exp: A derived attribute's value can be computed from other stored attributes; it is drawn with a dashed ellipse.

questions.q:
Statement I: A primary key attribute cannot contain NULL values.
Statement II: A relation can have more than one primary key but only one candidate key.
Which is correct?
options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false
Statement I is false and Statement II is true
questions.exp: Entity integrity forbids NULL in a primary key. A relation has exactly one primary key but may have several candidate keys, so II is false.

questions.q: A cascading rollback occurs when
options: a transaction is rolled back after all its locks are released
the failure of one transaction forces the rollback of other transactions that read its uncommitted data
two transactions request the same lock
questions.exp: If Ti aborts, any Tj that read Ti's uncommitted writes must also abort, possibly triggering a chain of rollbacks.

questions.q: Table Emp(dept) holds the values CS, EE, CS, ME, EE, NULL. What does SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT dept) FROM Emp return?
questions.exp: The distinct non-NULL values are CS, EE and ME, so the count is 3. COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column) ignore NULL values.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D) has the FDs AB → C and B → D, and AB is the only candidate key. The highest normal form satisfied is
questions.exp: B → D is a partial dependency of non-prime D on part of the key AB, violating 2NF; hence R is only in 1NF.

questions.q: Which of the following relational algebra equivalences is correct?
options: σ_c(R × S) = σ_c(R) × S for any condition c
questions.exp: Selection conditions can be cascaded. Projection distributes over union, not intersection; set difference is not commutative; the last holds only if c uses attributes of R alone.

questions.q: A foreign key column in a child table
options: can contain only values present in the parent key, or NULL
must be declared as the primary key of the child
questions.exp: Referential integrity requires each non-NULL foreign key value to match an existing parent key value; NULL is allowed unless declared NOT NULL.

questions.q: When a one-to-many relationship between Dept (one) and Emp (many) is converted to relational tables, the usual approach is to
options: add the primary key of Dept as a foreign key in the Emp table
add the primary key of Emp as a foreign key in the Dept table
create a third table with no keys
merge Dept and Emp into one table with a repeating group
questions.exp: The foreign key goes on the 'many' side, so each Emp row stores the Dept it belongs to.

questions.q: In data warehousing, ETL stands for
questions.exp: ETL extracts data from source systems, transforms it to a common format and loads it into the warehouse.

questions.q: A relation with 5 attributes and 7 tuples has
questions.exp: Degree is the number of attributes (columns) and cardinality is the number of tuples (rows).

questions.q: R(Student, Course, Instructor) has FDs (Student, Course) → Instructor and Instructor → Course. Which statement is correct?
options: R is in 3NF but not in BCNF; its BCNF decomposition is lossless but does not preserve (Student, Course) → Instructor
Every BCNF decomposition of R preserves all the dependencies
questions.exp: Candidate keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor), so Course is prime and 3NF holds; but Instructor → Course has a non-key determinant, violating BCNF. Splitting into (Instructor, Course) and (Student, Instructor) is lossless but loses the first FD.

questions.q: Marks(sid, sub, m) = (1,M,80), (1,P,70), (2,M,60), (2,P,90), (3,M,50). What does SELECT sid FROM Marks GROUP BY sid HAVING AVG(m) > 70 return?
questions.exp: Averages: sid 1 = 75, sid 2 = 75, sid 3 = 50. Sids 1 and 2 exceed 70.

questions.q: Table T(a, b) = (1,NULL), (2,3). What does SELECT SUM(a + b) FROM T return?
questions.exp: a + b gives NULL for the first row and 5 for the second; SUM ignores NULLs, so the result is 5.

questions.q: Table T(x) holds the values 1, 2, 2, 3, NULL. How many rows does SELECT * FROM T WHERE x <> 2 return?
questions.exp: Only 1 and 3 satisfy x <> 2. The comparison NULL <> 2 evaluates to UNKNOWN, so the NULL row is excluded: 2 rows.

questions.q: In two-phase locking, the lock point of a transaction is
options: the instant at which it commits
the instant at which it releases its first lock after commit
the instant at which it obtains its last lock, ending the growing phase
the instant at which it requests its first lock
questions.exp: The lock point separates the growing and shrinking phases; the equivalent serial order of 2PL transactions follows their lock points.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An aggregate function such as SUM() cannot be used directly in a WHERE clause.
Reason (R): WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and aggregation take place.
options: Both A and R are false
A is true and R is false
A is false and R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
questions.exp: WHERE is evaluated per row before GROUP BY, so aggregates are unavailable there; HAVING is used for conditions on groups.

questions.q: In the two-phase commit (2PC) protocol, what happens in the first (prepare / voting) phase?
options: Each participant acquires all its locks and then releases them (growing and shrinking phases)
The coordinator writes the global commit record and orders all participants to commit
The coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit, and each replies YES (ready) or NO (abort)
Participants copy their changes to a backup site and the coordinator deletes the log
questions.exp: Phase 1 is the voting phase: the coordinator sends PREPARE and participants force their log and answer VOTE-COMMIT (ready) or VOTE-ABORT. The decision (global commit or abort) is made in phase 2.

questions.q: Which statement about a B+ tree is correct?
options: Data records are stored only in the root node
Every internal node stores the data pointers for all its keys
The tree is always a binary tree
All keys with their data pointers appear in the leaf nodes, which are linked to support range scans
questions.exp: In a B+ tree, all search keys with data pointers are in the leaves, and leaves are chained in sequence, making range queries efficient.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about functional dependencies is correct (by Armstrong's axioms)?
options: If A → B then B → A
If A → B and A → C then A → BC
If A → BC then B → A
If AB → C then A → C
questions.exp: The union rule (derived from Armstrong's axioms) states A → B and A → C imply A → BC. The others are not valid inferences.

questions.q: The write-ahead logging (WAL) protocol requires that
options: data is written to disk only after the transaction ends
the log is never written to disk
the log record describing an update be written to stable storage before the updated data page is written to disk
commit records are written after checkpoints only
questions.exp: WAL ensures undo/redo information reaches stable storage before the modified page, enabling recovery.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has the FD A → B. Which decomposition is lossless?
questions.exp: For {AB, AC} the common attribute A is a key of AB (A → B), so the join is lossless. The others share B, C or nothing, with no key.

questions.q: Which SQL command is used to undo all changes made by the current transaction since its last commit?
questions.exp: ROLLBACK is the TCL command that aborts the transaction and restores the last committed state.

questions.q: Which of the following is always achievable for any relation schema?
options: A lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF
A lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF
A decomposition into 5NF that preserves all dependencies
questions.exp: The 3NF synthesis algorithm always gives a lossless, dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition; BCNF cannot always preserve dependencies.

questions.q: Data redundancy, data inconsistency and difficulty in concurrent access are typical problems of
questions.exp: Traditional file systems keep separate files per application, causing duplicated data, inconsistencies and poor concurrency control, which a DBMS is designed to solve.

questions.q: S(dept, gender) = (CS,M), (CS,F), (CS,M), (EE,M), (EE,M). How many rows are returned by SELECT dept, gender, COUNT(*) FROM S GROUP BY dept, gender?
questions.exp: The distinct (dept, gender) combinations are (CS,M), (CS,F) and (EE,M): 3 groups.

questions.q:
Statement I: Every relation with only two attributes is in BCNF.
Statement II: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF.
options: Statement I is false and Statement II is true
Statement I is true and Statement II is false
questions.exp: With two attributes every non-trivial FD has a key as determinant, so BCNF holds. BCNF is stronger than 3NF, so II is false.

questions.q: R(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade) has key (StudentID, CourseID). Which dependency causes a 2NF violation?
questions.exp: StudentName depends on StudentID, which is only part of the key (a partial dependency), violating 2NF.

questions.q: A relation R(A, B, C) has two candidate keys, A and B (each a single attribute). How many superkeys does R have?
questions.exp: Of the 8 subsets of {A,B,C}, only those containing neither A nor B (the empty set and {C}) are not superkeys. 8 − 2 = 6.

questions.q: A(id) = {1,2,3} and B(id) = {2,3,4}. How many rows does SELECT * FROM A RIGHT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id return?
questions.exp: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of B: ids 2 and 3 match; id 4 appears with NULLs for A. Total 3 rows (id 1 of A is dropped).

questions.q: Predicting whether a loan applicant will default (yes/no) using past labeled records is an example of
questions.exp: Assigning an item to one of predefined classes using labeled training data is classification.

questions.q: A weak entity set
options: is identified by a partial key (discriminator) together with the primary key of its owner entity
has a primary key made of its own attributes only
can exist without any relationship to another entity set
questions.exp: A weak entity lacks a full key of its own; its discriminator combined with the owner's key identifies it.

questions.q: In an ER diagram, an identifying relationship (between a weak entity and its owner) is represented by
questions.exp: A weak entity set is drawn with a double rectangle and its identifying relationship with a double diamond.

questions.q: A natural join differs from an equi-join in that the natural join
options: uses an inequality condition such as <
automatically equates all attributes with the same name and keeps one copy of each in the result
questions.exp: Natural join = equi-join on all common attributes followed by dropping the duplicate columns; a general equi-join keeps both columns.

questions.q: In the transaction state diagram, a transaction enters the 'partially committed' state
options: after its final statement has been executed
after the data is written to the log and the DB is closed
questions.exp: Active → partially committed occurs after the last statement executes; it becomes committed only after the changes are safely recorded.
Division returns A-values paired with every B in S: a1 (b1,b2) and a3 (b1,b2) qualify; a2 has only b1.

questions.q: In 2PC the coordinator decides GLOBAL-COMMIT only if
options: a majority of the participants have voted YES
at least one participant has voted YES
the coordinator itself has finished its local work, whatever the votes are
questions.exp: 2PC needs unanimity: a single NO vote (or a missing vote after a timeout) forces GLOBAL-ABORT; commit requires all participants to be ready.

questions.q: Converting a 2NF relation to 3NF involves eliminating
options: transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on the key
questions.exp: 2NF already removes partial dependencies; 3NF removes transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on candidate keys.

questions.q: In the growing phase of two-phase locking, a transaction
options: may obtain locks but may not release any lock
may release locks but not obtain any
may neither obtain nor release locks
must release all locks at once
questions.exp: 2PL has a growing phase (acquire only) followed by a shrinking phase (release only).

questions.q: In a star schema, the central table is the
options: lookup table that stores only text descriptions
fact table, surrounded by dimension tables
questions.exp: A star schema has a central fact table of measures and foreign keys linked to surrounding dimension tables.

questions.q: When a multivalued attribute of an entity is converted to the relational model, it is represented by
options: a separate relation containing the entity's key and the attribute
questions.exp: A multivalued attribute becomes a new relation with the owner's primary key plus the attribute, one row per value.

questions.q: In the three-schema architecture, the level that describes how data is physically stored is the
questions.exp: The internal schema describes physical storage structures and access paths; conceptual describes the whole logical database; external describes user views.

questions.q: Adding a new attribute to a table in the conceptual schema without having to rewrite existing application programs that use views is an example of
questions.exp: Logical data independence is the capacity to change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or application programs.

questions.q: In timestamp ordering, transaction T with TS(T) = 5 tries to read item X whose write-timestamp W-TS(X) = 8. What happens?
options: T is rolled back because it would read a value written by a younger transaction
T reads X and R-TS(X) becomes 5
T waits until the writer commits
T is allowed and W-TS(X) is reset to 5
questions.exp: The rule is: if TS(T) < W-TS(X), the read is rejected and T is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp.

questions.q: Relation R(A, B, C) has A as its only candidate key. How many super keys does R have?
questions.exp: Every super key must contain A; the other two attributes B and C may be present or absent freely: 2^2 = 4 super keys (A, AB, AC, ABC).

questions.q: Given Enrolled(sid, cid), which expression returns the sids of students who took BOTH C1 and C2?
questions.exp: A single tuple cannot have two cid values, so the AND selection is empty. Intersecting the sids for C1 and C2 gives students with both.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has FDs AB → C and C → B. R is decomposed into R1(A, C) and R2(C, B). Which statement is correct?
options: The decomposition is lossy and dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossy and not dependency preserving
The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving
questions.exp: R1 ∩ R2 = C and C → B, so C is a key of R2: lossless. But AB → C cannot be derived from the FDs of R1 and R2, so it is not dependency preserving.

questions.q: In SQL, a view is best described as
options: a physical copy of a table stored on a different disk
an index on a primary key
a virtual table defined by a stored query
questions.exp: A view stores a query definition, not data, and presents its result as a virtual relation.

questions.q: Schedule S: r1(X) w2(X) r2(Y) w1(Y). Which statement is correct?
options: S is conflict serializable as T1 then T2
S is conflict serializable as T2 then T1
questions.exp: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 → T2; r2(Y) before w1(Y) gives T2 → T1. The precedence graph has a cycle, so it is not conflict serializable.

questions.q: In a data warehouse, a fact table typically contains
options: numeric measures (such as sales amount) and foreign keys to dimension tables
only the primary keys of source systems
questions.exp: Fact tables store measurable quantities at a chosen granularity, together with keys linking to the dimension tables.

questions.q: In a specialization, if an entity can belong to more than one lower-level entity set at the same time (e.g. a person who is both a student and an employee), the specialization is
questions.exp: Overlapping specialization allows an entity in several sub-classes; disjoint allows at most one.

questions.q: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and
options: no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key
questions.exp: 2NF removes partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on a proper subset of a candidate key.

questions.q: For R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E, E → A}, the closure {D}+ is
questions.exp: D → E, E → A, A → B gives {D, E, A, B}. C cannot be derived, so BC → D is not triggered and closure is {A, B, D, E}.

questions.q: A relationship set that involves three entity sets is called a
questions.exp: The degree of a relationship set is the number of participating entity sets: 1 = unary, 2 = binary, 3 = ternary.

questions.q: Which SQL constraint can enforce that a column 'age' must always be greater than 0?
questions.exp: CHECK (age > 0) restricts the values that may be stored in the column.

questions.q: For three transactions T1, T2 and T3, the number of possible serial schedules is
questions.exp: Serial schedules correspond to orderings of the transactions: 3! = 6.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a relation in the relational model?
options: Tuples are ordered by their insertion time
Each attribute has a name that is unique within the relation
questions.exp: A relation is a set of tuples, so tuple order is immaterial; insertion order is not a property of a relation.

questions.q:
Dept(did) = 10, 20, 30; Emp(eid, did) = (1,10), (2,10), (3,30). What does this return?
SELECT did FROM Dept d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Emp e WHERE e.did = d.did);
questions.exp: Departments 10 and 30 have employees. Only department 20 has no matching Emp row, so NOT EXISTS is true for it.

questions.q: In multiple-granularity locking, an intention-exclusive (IX) lock on a table means that the transaction
options: intends to set exclusive locks on some rows within the table
has locked the whole table exclusively
only wants to read the table
questions.exp: IX indicates an intention to take X locks at a finer level (rows) below this node; it does not itself lock the whole table.

questions.q: Which SQL statement sets an intermediate point within a transaction to which one can later roll back partially?
questions.exp: SAVEPOINT marks a point in the transaction; ROLLBACK TO savepoint undoes only later changes.

questions.q: A relation is in BCNF if and only if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds in it,
options: X is a proper subset of a candidate key
Y is a subset of X
questions.exp: BCNF requires the determinant of every non-trivial FD to be a superkey.

questions.q: Names in table P: Anil, Sunil, Anita, Nila, Anand. How many rows does SELECT * FROM P WHERE name LIKE '_n%' return?
questions.exp: The pattern needs 'n' as the second character: Anil, Anita and Anand match; Sunil (u), Nila (i) do not. So 3.

questions.q: In relational algebra, the rename operator is written
questions.exp: ρ renames a relation or its attributes; σ selects rows, π projects columns, ⋈ is join.

questions.q: The mapping between the external level and the conceptual level in the three-schema architecture is mainly what supports
questions.exp: Mapping external views to the conceptual schema lets the conceptual schema change without rewriting user views (logical independence); the conceptual-internal mapping gives physical independence.

questions.q: T(c) = A, B, A, C, B. What does SELECT c FROM T GROUP BY c HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; return?
questions.exp: A appears twice, B twice and C once; only A and B have count above 1.

questions.q: Emp(eid, did) has a foreign key did referencing Dept(did) declared with ON DELETE CASCADE. What happens when a Dept row is deleted?
options: did in the Emp rows is set to its default only
All Emp rows referencing that department are also deleted
questions.exp: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates the deletion to the referencing child rows to preserve referential integrity.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has primary key A and tuples (1,2,3), (2,2,3), (3,NULL,4). Which insertion will be accepted?
questions.exp: (1,9,9) and (2,2,3) duplicate existing key values and (NULL,1,1) has a NULL key. (4,2,3) has a new non-null key, so it is accepted.

questions.q: Rigorous two-phase locking differs from strict two-phase locking in that rigorous 2PL holds
options: all locks, shared as well as exclusive, until the transaction commits or aborts
no locks after the first read
locks only during the growing phase
questions.exp: Strict 2PL keeps only exclusive locks until the end; rigorous 2PL keeps both shared and exclusive locks, so transactions are serialised in commit order.

questions.q: Which protocol makes a distributed transaction either commit at all participating sites or abort at all of them?
questions.exp: Two-phase commit is the atomic commit protocol (voting then decision). 2PL and timestamp ordering provide serializability, wait-die is deadlock prevention.

questions.q: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the functional dependencies A → B and B → C, and A is the only candidate key. The highest normal form of R is
questions.exp: The key is a single attribute so no partial dependency exists (2NF), but B → C is a transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute, so R is not in 3NF.

questions.q: A(x) = {1,2,3}, B(y) = {2,3,4}. How many rows does SELECT x FROM A UNION SELECT y FROM B return?
questions.exp: UNION removes duplicates, leaving the distinct values 1, 2, 3, 4: 4 rows (UNION ALL would give 6).

questions.q:
T(x) = 5, 10, 15. What does this return?
SELECT x FROM T WHERE x > ANY (SELECT x FROM T WHERE x <= 10);
questions.exp: The subquery returns {5, 10}. x > ANY means greater than at least one value, i.e. greater than 5: so 10 and 15 qualify.

questions.q: According to Thomas' write rule in timestamp ordering, if TS(T) < W-TS(X) and T attempts to write X, the system
options: ignores the obsolete write and lets T continue
questions.exp: Thomas' write rule skips outdated writes instead of aborting the transaction, increasing concurrency.

questions.q: Which isolation level is the weakest, permitting dirty reads?
questions.exp: READ UNCOMMITTED lets a transaction read data not yet committed by others (dirty reads); the other levels prevent it.

questions.q: Transaction T1 runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM P WHERE age > 30 twice. In between, T2 inserts a new row with age 40 and commits, so T1 sees different counts. This anomaly is called
questions.exp: A phantom read occurs when a repeated range query returns new rows inserted by another committed transaction.

questions.q:
Statement I: Many NoSQL systems always provide full ACID transactions across the whole cluster.
Statement II: Many NoSQL systems offer eventual consistency to gain availability and scalability.
options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false
Statement I is false and Statement II is true
questions.exp: Many distributed NoSQL stores relax strict ACID and offer eventual consistency (BASE), so I is false and II is true.

questions.q: In the relational model, a foreign key is
options: an attribute that is unique and never NULL in its own relation
any attribute that appears in more than one relation
an attribute (or set) in one relation that refers to the primary key of another (or the same) relation
the attribute chosen to sort tuples physically
questions.exp: A foreign key references a candidate/primary key of a referenced relation and enforces referential integrity.

questions.q: In the wait-die deadlock prevention scheme, T1 (timestamp 5) requests an item held by T2 (timestamp 10). What happens?
options: T1 waits, because it is older
T1 is aborted, because it is older
T2 is aborted and T1 proceeds immediately
questions.exp: In wait-die an older requester waits for a younger holder; a younger requester would die (be rolled back).

questions.q: By the pseudo-transitivity rule, if X → Y and WY → Z then
questions.exp: From X → Y, augment with W: WX → WY; with WY → Z, transitivity gives WX → Z.

questions.q: In a canonical (minimal) cover of a set of functional dependencies, every dependency has
options: the whole relation on its right-hand side
only prime attributes on its left side
a single attribute on its right-hand side, with no extraneous attribute and no redundant dependency
a candidate key on its left side
questions.exp: A canonical cover is obtained by splitting right sides to single attributes, removing extraneous left-side attributes and deleting redundant FDs; it is the starting point of 3NF synthesis.

questions.q: In ER modelling, aggregation is used to
options: compute the sum of an attribute
treat a relationship set as an abstract entity so that it can take part in another relationship
merge two entity sets into one table
convert a weak entity into a strong entity
questions.exp: Aggregation abstracts a relationship (with its participating entities) into a higher-level entity that can participate in further relationships.

questions.q: For the M:N relationship set between entity sets E1 and E2, the primary key of the relationship's relation consists of
options: the primary key of E1 only
the union of the primary keys of E1 and E2
the primary key of E2 only
questions.exp: In an M:N relationship a pair of entity instances identifies a relationship instance, so the combined keys form the key.

questions.q: R(A, B) = {(1,x), (2,y), (3,x)}. The number of tuples in π_B(R) is
questions.exp: Projection removes duplicates; the distinct B values are x and y, so 2 tuples.

questions.q: After a money transfer between two accounts, the combined balance of both accounts has changed. Which ACID property has been violated?
questions.exp: Consistency requires transactions to take the database from one valid state to another; a changed total breaks the integrity rule that the sum stays the same.

questions.q: A B+ tree allows at most 3 keys per node. When a leaf overflows (4 keys) it splits into two leaves of 2 keys each. Keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are inserted in order. How many leaf nodes exist at the end?
questions.exp: Leaves split at 1-4 into [1,2],[3,4]; at 6 [3,4,5,6] splits into [3,4],[5,6]; 7 goes into [5,6,7]. Final leaves: [1,2],[3,4],[5,6,7] = 3.

questions.q: In an ER diagram, a diamond shape represents a
questions.exp: Rectangles denote entity sets, ellipses attributes and diamonds relationship sets.

questions.q: Relation R has 5 tuples and relation S has 4 tuples. How many tuples are there in R × S?
questions.exp: Cartesian product pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S: 5 × 4 = 20.

questions.q:
Table Sales(region, amt): (E,10), (E,20), (W,5), (W,15), (W,25), (N,30). What is the result of
SELECT region, SUM(amt) FROM Sales GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amt) > 30;
questions.exp: Sums: E = 30, W = 45, N = 30. HAVING keeps only groups with sum > 30, which is W.

questions.q: In specialization with attribute inheritance, a lower-level entity set
options: inherits all attributes and relationships of its higher-level entity set
inherits only the key of its parent and nothing else
cannot have attributes of its own
must have exactly the same number of attributes as its parent
questions.exp: Attribute inheritance means lower-level entities automatically have the attributes (and participate in relationships) of the higher-level entity set, in addition to their own.

questions.q: A 1:1 relationship between entity sets E1 and E2 with total participation on both sides is best mapped to the relational model by
options: merging both entity sets (and the relationship) into a single relation
creating three relations: E1, E2 and a relationship relation with a composite key
creating two relations with no foreign key
creating a relation only for the relationship, dropping the entity sets
questions.exp: With total participation on both sides of a 1:1 relationship, one table holding all attributes of both entity sets avoids joins and keeps the constraint (the other options lose information or are unnecessary).

questions.q:
Orders(oid, cust, amt): (1,A,100), (2,B,50), (3,A,200), (4,C,70), (5,B,150). What does this return?
SELECT cust, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY cust ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, cust ASC LIMIT 1;
questions.exp: Counts: A = 2, B = 2, C = 1. Sorting by count descending then name ascending puts A first, so (A, 2).

questions.q: For F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}, how many functional dependencies are there in a minimal (canonical) cover of F?
questions.exp: Split A → BC; A → C and AB → C are redundant (A → B → C). The minimal cover is {A → B, B → C}: 2 dependencies.

questions.q: R(A, B) = {(1,x), (2,y)} and S(B, C) = {(x,p), (z,q)}. How many tuples of R left outer join S contain a NULL?
questions.exp: The result is (1,x,p) and (2,y,NULL). Only the tuple for (2,y) has a NULL, so 1.
π_A(R) = {1,2,3} (3 tuples) and π_B(R) = {2,3} (2 tuples), so the product has 3 × 2 = 6 tuples.

questions.q: Inserting a tuple with NULL in its primary key attribute violates
questions.exp: The entity integrity constraint states that no primary key attribute may be NULL.

questions.q: A disk block is 1024 bytes. A key takes 8 bytes and a pointer takes 8 bytes. What is the maximum number of pointers (order p) an internal B+ tree node can hold if it has p pointers and p − 1 keys?

Emp(eid, did) = (1,10), (2,20), (3,NULL); Dept(did, dname) = (10,X), (20,Y), (30,Z). How many rows does this return?
SELECT * FROM Emp e LEFT JOIN Dept d ON e.did = d.did WHERE d.did IS NULL;
questions.exp: LEFT JOIN keeps all 3 employees; only employee 3 has a NULL did and finds no match, giving d.did NULL. So 1 row.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a database schema from a database instance?
options: The schema is the data currently stored; the instance is the structure of the tables
The schema is the physical file layout; the instance is the set of views
Both terms mean the same thing; they differ only in the DBMS product
The schema is the logical structure (relations, attributes, domains) and changes rarely; the instance is the data stored at a given moment
questions.exp: Schema = design (like a class definition) and is stable; instance = snapshot of the tuples at a time (like the objects) and changes with every insert, delete or update.

questions.q: Table Emp(id, sal) contains rows (1,100), (2,200), (3,NULL), (4,200). What does SELECT COUNT(sal), COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT sal) FROM Emp return?
questions.exp: COUNT(sal) ignores NULL giving 3; COUNT(*) counts all 4 rows; DISTINCT non-null sal values are 100 and 200, so 2.

questions.q: A cycle in the wait-for graph of a lock-based system indicates
questions.exp: A cycle means each transaction in it waits for a lock held by another in the cycle, i.e. a deadlock.

questions.q: Given Student(sid, name, dept) and Enrolled(sid, cid), which expression gives the names of students enrolled in course 'C1'?
questions.exp: Join Student and Enrolled on sid, select cid = 'C1', then project name. The first option fails because cid is not available after projecting name.

questions.q: A relation is in 3NF if for every non-trivial FD X → A, either X is a superkey or
options: A is a subset of X only
questions.exp: The 3NF condition is that X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key).

questions.q: A recursive relationship in an ER model is one in which
options: an entity set participates more than once, in different roles, in the same relationship set
questions.exp: In a recursive (unary) relationship, such as an employee supervising another employee, one entity set plays multiple roles.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D) has FDs AB → C, C → D and D → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.exp: B is in every key. AB → C → D gives all attributes; BC: C → D → A; BD: D → A. Keys: AB, BC, BD = 3.

questions.q: For R(A, B, C), which expression is invalid?
questions.exp: After π_A(R) only attribute A remains, so a selection on B cannot be applied.

questions.q: Dividing a relation into subsets of its tuples (rows) that are stored at different sites of a distributed database is called
questions.exp: Horizontal fragmentation splits by rows (selection); vertical fragmentation splits by columns (projection); replication stores copies.

questions.q: Which SQL statement adds a new column email to an existing table Student?
options: UPDATE TABLE Student ADD email VARCHAR(50);
INSERT INTO Student ADD email VARCHAR(50);
ALTER TABLE Student ADD email VARCHAR(50);
questions.exp: Structure changes use the DDL command ALTER TABLE ... ADD. UPDATE and INSERT change rows, not table structure, and MODIFY TABLE is not standard SQL.

questions.q: Two operations from different transactions are in conflict when they access the same data item and at least one is a write. Which pair is in conflict?
questions.exp: W1(X) and R2(X) are on the same item X, from different transactions, and one is a write, so they conflict. The others lack one of these conditions.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D) has FDs A → B and B → C. What is the highest normal form of R?
questions.exp: The only candidate key is AD (closure of AD is ABCD). Non-prime attribute B depends on A, a proper part of the key, so a partial dependency exists: R is not in 2NF and is only in 1NF.

questions.q: A table has a column Phone storing values like '98765, 91234' in a single cell. This design violates
questions.exp: 1NF requires atomic (indivisible) attribute values; storing several phone numbers in one cell breaks it.

questions.q: The theta-join R ⋈_θ S is equivalent to
questions.exp: A theta join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection with condition θ.

questions.q: Log: <T1 start>, <T1, A, 10, 20>, <T1 commit>, <T2 start>, <T2, B, 5, 8>. The system crashes now. During recovery
options: both T1 and T2 are redone
both T1 and T2 are undone
T1 is undone and T2 is redone
T1 is redone and T2 is undone
questions.exp: T1 committed before the crash so its update is redone; T2 has no commit record, so its update is undone.

questions.q: Relation R(A, B, C) has A as its only candidate key. Which of the following sets of attributes is NOT a superkey?
questions.exp: A superkey must contain a candidate key. {B, C} lacks A, so it is not a superkey.

questions.q: Which statement distinguishes a B-tree from a B+ tree?
options: A B+ tree stores no keys in internal nodes
A B-tree can store data pointers in internal nodes as well as leaves, while a B+ tree keeps them only in leaves
A B-tree is always shorter than a B+ tree
questions.exp: In a B-tree each key appears once and may carry a data pointer at any level; in a B+ tree data pointers are only in the leaves and internal keys are copies for routing.

questions.q: In an ER diagram, total participation of an entity set in a relationship is shown by
questions.exp: A double line from the entity to the relationship means every entity must participate; a single line means partial participation.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D) has FDs A → B and C → D, with AC as the only key. Using the 3NF synthesis algorithm, the minimum number of relations in the decomposition is
questions.exp: Relations (A,B) and (C,D) come from the FDs; neither contains the key AC, so a third relation (A,C) is added: 3.

questions.q: Physical data independence refers to the ability to
options: add new attributes without changing application programs
change the physical storage structures or access paths without changing the conceptual schema
change the external views without changing storage
run programs on any hardware without recompilation
questions.exp: Physical data independence means changes at the internal (storage) level do not require changes in the conceptual schema.

questions.q:
Table Stu(name, marks): (A,40), (B,60), (C,80), (D,60). What does this query return?
SELECT name FROM Stu WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM Stu);
questions.exp: AVG = (40+60+80+60)/4 = 60. Only marks strictly greater than 60 qualify, which is C (80).

questions.q: If relations R(A, B) and S(C, D) have no attribute in common, then the natural join R ⋈ S is equivalent to
options: the union of R and S
questions.exp: With no common attributes there is nothing to equate, so every pair combines: the Cartesian product.

questions.q: Given Student(sid, name) and Enrolled(sid, cid), which expression gives the sids of students not enrolled in any course?
questions.exp: Set difference of all student ids minus ids that appear in Enrolled leaves the students with no enrollment.

questions.q: A file has 10,000 records and a block holds 50 records. A sparse primary index has one entry per data block. How many index entries are needed?
questions.exp: Number of blocks = 10000 / 50 = 200, so a sparse index has 200 entries (a dense index would need 10,000).

questions.q: Which pair of locks on the same data item, held by different transactions, are compatible?
questions.exp: Multiple transactions may read together, so shared-shared is the only compatible combination.

questions.q: In the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture, the level that describes only the part of the database relevant to a particular group of users is the
options: storage level of the operating system
questions.exp: The external level contains many user views, each showing only the data of interest to one user group; the conceptual level gives the whole logical design and the internal level the physical storage.

questions.q: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has the functional dependencies AB → CD and C → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.exp: B is on no right side so it is in every key. AB is a key, and since C → A, BC also determines A and hence everything. A+ = A and B+ = B, so the keys are AB and BC: 2.

questions.q: Items(id, qty) = (1,5), (2,NULL), (3,7). What does SELECT AVG(qty) FROM Items return?
questions.exp: AVG ignores NULLs: (5 + 7) / 2 = 6, not 12/3.

questions.q: A bank transfers Rs 500 from account A to B. The system crashes after A is debited but before B is credited. On restart A's debit is undone. Which ACID property ensures this?
questions.exp: Atomicity makes the transfer all-or-nothing, so the partial debit is rolled back.

questions.q:
P(id, price): (1,10), (2,30), (3,20). What does this return?
SELECT id FROM P WHERE price = (SELECT MAX(price) FROM P WHERE price < (SELECT MAX(price) FROM P));
questions.exp: Innermost MAX = 30; next MAX of prices below 30 is 20, which belongs to id 3 (second highest price).

questions.q: R(A, B, C) satisfies A → B, B → C and C → A. How many candidate keys does it have?
questions.exp: A+, B+ and C+ each equal {A,B,C}, so A, B and C are each candidate keys: 3.

questions.q: Tables A(id) = {1,2,3} and B(id) = {2,3,4}. How many rows does SELECT * FROM A FULL OUTER JOIN B ON A.id = B.id return?
questions.exp: Matches: 2 and 3 (2 rows). Unmatched A row 1 and unmatched B row 4 add 2 more rows: 4 in total.

questions.q: T(a, b) = (1,10), (2,20), (3,30), (4,40). What does SELECT SUM(b) FROM T WHERE a BETWEEN 2 AND 3; return?
questions.exp: BETWEEN is inclusive, so rows with a = 2 and 3 qualify: 20 + 30 = 50.

questions.q: Fourth normal form (4NF) is concerned with the elimination of
questions.exp: 4NF extends BCNF by removing non-trivial multivalued dependencies whose determinant is not a superkey.

questions.q: A major advantage of strict two-phase locking is that
options: it removes the need for a recovery manager
it avoids cascading rollbacks because exclusive locks are held until commit or abort
questions.exp: Holding write locks until the end means no other transaction reads uncommitted data, so cascading aborts cannot occur.

questions.q: R(A,B,C,D,E,F) has FDs AB → C, BC → AD, D → E, CF → B. The closure {A, B}+ is
questions.exp: AB → C gives ABC; BC → AD adds D; D → E adds E. F is never derived, so the closure is {A, B, C, D, E}.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of relations (tables) needed to represent two entity sets E1 and E2 connected by a many-to-many relationship in the relational model?
questions.exp: One table per entity set plus a separate table for the M:N relationship holding both foreign keys: 3.

questions.q: In an ER diagram, an attribute that can hold more than one value for a single entity (for example, several phone numbers of one person) is called a
questions.exp: An attribute that can store a set of values for one entity is multivalued; it is drawn with a double ellipse.

questions.q:
Match the SQL statements with their categories.
1. CREATE  2. INSERT  3. GRANT  4. COMMIT
P. DCL  Q. TCL  R. DDL  S. DML
questions.exp: CREATE is DDL, INSERT is DML, GRANT is DCL and COMMIT is TCL.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental (primitive) operator of relational algebra?
questions.exp: Fundamental operators are select, project, union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename; intersection can be derived as R − (R − S).

questions.q: Which statement about schedules is correct?
options: Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, and a view-serializable schedule that is not conflict serializable must contain blind writes
Blind writes never occur in any schedule
questions.exp: Conflict serializability implies view serializability; the converse fails only in the presence of blind writes (writes without a prior read).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ER model?
questions.exp: A tuple is a relational-model term; entities, weak entities, relationships and attributes belong to the ER model.

questions.q: The ACID property that guarantees that once a transaction has committed its changes survive system crashes is
questions.exp: Durability means committed updates persist even after failures, usually via logging to stable storage.
